# 📌 TOPIC 1 — Why Learn Git in an MLOps Module?

**Question from a learner:** *Git seems simple. Shouldn't it be taught at the start of the course?*

**Answer:**
- Git was covered **briefly after Python**, but not in depth for everyone.
- **Most people (including the tutor) never took a proper Git course.** They learn only what they use at work and "work their way around it".
- In MLOps, Git is used every day for:
  - **Contributing** code
  - **Fixing bugs**
  - **Understanding** someone else's code
  - **Documenting** the project (README)
  - **CI/CD** (automatic testing & deployment; covered later)
- So it is part of the MLOps curriculum.

> 💡 **Real-world fact:** In most serious companies, code **never sits on your laptop**. Many companies don't even allow cloning code to your local machine; you work **only on a cloud machine**.

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 1 — Why Learn Git in an MLOps Module?**

# 📌 TOPIC 2 — Git vs GitHub

**Are Git and GitHub the same thing?** ❌ **No.**

| | Git | GitHub |
|---|---|---|
| **What** | An **open-source Version Control System (VCS)** | A **product/service** that hosts Git repositories online |
| **Who owns it** | Open source (free for everyone) | **Microsoft** |
| **Analogy** | **Email** (the technology) | **Gmail** (a company providing email as a service) |

### Email Analogy

```
Technology       Companies that provide it as a service
─────────────    ──────────────────────────────────────────
Email      ───►  Gmail, Yahoo, Zepto Mail, Proton
Git        ───►  GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, CodeCommit
```

### Companies Providing "Git as a Service"

| Service | Owned by |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Microsoft |
| **GitLab** | GitLab Inc. |
| **Bitbucket** | Atlassian |
| **CodeCommit** | Amazon (AWS); used inside AWS infrastructure |

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 2 — Git vs GitHub**

# 📌 TOPIC 3 — What Version Control Does: Commit = Snapshot

**Situation:** Your project is **stable** and working fine. Now you want to add a new feature **without breaking the stable version**.

```
Current file  ●━━━━━━━━[ Stable ]━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━►
                           │
                           ▼
                Commit = snapshot of the codebase
```

- **Without Git:** you would make a copy (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V) of the folder as a backup. Messy!
- **With Git:** you **commit**, which **saves a snapshot** of the whole codebase.
- You can **go back (revert)** to any snapshot at any time.
- So you can modify code freely, **without fear of losing your work**.

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 3 — What Version Control Does: Commit = Snapshot**

# 📌 TOPIC 4 — Types of Version Control Systems

![Centralized vs Distributed VCS](images/vcs_centralized_vs_distributed.png)

### 4.1 Centralized Version Control System (CVCS)

**How it works:**
- There is **one central server** with the **only copy** of the code.
- Developers (e.g., Tulasi, Rajesh, Koushal, Shubham) **log in, work, and log out**.
- **No developer gets a copy** on their computer.
- **Only ONE person can make changes at a time** (no concurrency).

| ✅ Pros | ❌ Cons |
|---|---|
| **Maximum / high security**: all code stays on one server | **Single point of failure**: server goes down → everything is lost (no backup) |
| You know **exactly who logged in, when, and what they changed** | **Not scalable**: impossible with thousands of developers |
| **No conflicts**: only one person edits at a time | **No offline work**: must always be connected |
| **Real-time** updates and monitoring | |

**When to use:** very high-security projects (e.g., **military-grade** applications). Rare, but it exists.

> 🎮 **Could GTA 6 be built this way?** No. Thousands of developers across the world work on it day and night. A centralized system can't scale to that.

### 4.2 Distributed Version Control System (DVCS), like Git

**How it works:**

```
Remote Server ──(copy/clone)──► Developer's copy ──(make changes)──► Modified copy
      ▲                                                                    │
      └──────────────────────────(update server / push)────────────────────┘
```

1. A **remote server** holds the main code.
2. Each developer **creates a full copy** on their computer.
3. They work on the copy (add features, fix bugs) → **modified copy**.
4. They **update the server** with their changes.

| ✅ Pros | ❌ Cons |
|---|---|
| **Very scalable**: thousands of developers at once | **Security risk**: everyone has a full copy, so code can **leak** |
| Full copy of the code on your own computer | |
| Can work **offline** | |

> ⚠️ **Real example of the con:** The **entire source code of GTA 5** (one of the most popular and profitable games ever, with a budget of hundreds of millions of dollars) **was leaked on Christmas Eve 2023**. Leaks like that are extremely harmful to a company.

### 4.3 Quick Comparison

| | Centralized | Distributed (Git) |
|---|---|---|
| Copies of code | One (on server) | Everyone has one |
| People working at once | One | Many |
| Offline work | ❌ | ✅ |
| Scalable | ❌ | ✅ |
| Security | 🔒 Highest | ⚠️ Risk of leaks |
| Conflicts | Never | Possible (see Topic 10) |

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 4 — Types of Version Control Systems**

# 📌 TOPIC 5 — Git Terminology & Commands

### 5.1 Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Repository (repo)** | A **fancy word for a folder** that contains **code, documents** and important info. *(Not your hard disk full of movies!)* |
| **Local Repository** | The folder **on your computer**. It may or may not be synced with the remote repo. |
| **Remote Repository** | The **online copy** of your codebase (on GitHub). |

> "Repo" can mean the **local** or the **remote** one. Always be clear which one you mean.

### 5.2 Commands

![How a change travels in Git](images/git_add_commit_push.png)

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| **`git add`** | Adds file(s) to the **staging area** (picks which changes go into the next commit) |
| **`git commit`** | **Saves a snapshot** of the codebase in your **local** repo |
| **`git push`** | **Updates the remote repo** with new commits from your local repo |
| **`git fetch`** | **Downloads** the latest changes from the remote repo (does **not** change your files yet) |
| **`git pull`** | **Updates your local repo** with the remote repo (= fetch + merge) |
| **`git clone`** | Creates a **local copy** of a remote repository on your computer |

### 5.3 The Staging Area

```
git add File1 File2
        │
        ▼
 ┌──── Staging Area ────┐
 │   File1              │ ───► Commit ───► Push
 │   File2              │
 └──────────────────────┘
```

**The 3-step flow:**   **ADD → COMMIT → PUSH**

### 5.4 Commit vs Push (common confusion)

| | Commit | Push |
|---|---|---|
| Saves where? | **Local** repo (your computer) | **Remote** repo (GitHub) |
| Analogy | Taking a **screenshot** of the codebase | **Uploading** that screenshot online |
| Others can see it? | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |

> **Learner question:** *Does commit save to the local repo or the remote repo?*
> **Answer:** **Commit saves to the LOCAL repo.** Only **push** updates the remote one.

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 5 — Git Terminology & Commands**

**A good GitHub profile has:**
- A **profile README**: who you are, skills, past experience, publications

# 📌 TOPIC 7 — Hands-on: Create a Repo, Clone, Commit, Push (GitHub Desktop)

The tutor created the **class repository** (MLOps, September 2026 batch). **All future class notes and notebooks will be uploaded there.** 📌 **Bookmark the link** shared in class.

### 7.1 Create a Repository on GitHub

1. GitHub → **New**
2. Give it a **name**
3. Choose **Public** (anyone can see it) or **Private** (only you)
4. Template: none (for now)
5. **Create** → an empty repo now exists on your GitHub account

### 7.2 Clone It with GitHub Desktop

1. Download **GitHub Desktop** (Windows / Mac)
2. **Settings → Sign in** → authorize in the browser
3. **Add → Clone Repository** → choose your repo → pick a local folder → **Clone**
4. Click **Open in VS Code**

**What is cloning?** Creating a **local copy** of the **remote** repository on your computer.

**Why clone?** **All development happens locally first.** When it's done, you push to the remote repository.

### 7.3 First Commit: README.md

**Why README matters:** It is the **window into your project**: the problem, the approach, a quick start, and the contents. Everything a new user needs to know.

1. Create `README.md` in the folder
2. GitHub Desktop shows **"1 changed file"**
3. Write a **commit message** (be a bit descriptive, e.g., *"This is the first commit"*)
4. Click **Commit**
5. Click **Publish / Push** → the remote repo is updated

### 7.4 Empty Folders Are NOT Tracked

> ⚠️ Git **ignores empty folders**. To keep an empty folder in the repo, put an empty placeholder file in it, e.g. **`.gitkeep`**.

### 7.5 Why We Will Move to the Terminal Later

- We start with the **UI** because it is **easier to understand**.
- In future classes we use **only terminal commands**.
- **Why?** On **remote servers there is no UI**, only a terminal. You must be comfortable with Git commands.

> 🧙 *"Using the Git GUI? 10 points from Gryffindor!"*

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 7 — Hands-on: Create a Repo, Clone, Commit, Push (GitHub Desktop)**

# 📌 TOPIC 8 — Branches

![Branching and merging](images/git_branching.png)

### 8.1 What Is a Branch?

**A branch = a copy of the codebase** (copy of the folder). That's it.

**Why?**
- The **main / master** branch is the **stable, production** version. **Never experiment on it directly.**
- Create a branch (e.g., `v1`) → build the new feature there → each dot is a **commit**.
- Feature is good? → **merge** it into main.
- Feature is bad? → **delete the branch**. Main was never touched.

> **In short:** you don't want to "dirty" the production folder. Experiment in a separate copy, and merge only when you're happy.

### 8.2 Creating & Using a Branch (GitHub Desktop)

1. **Current Branch → New Branch** → name it `v1` → **Create Branch**
2. VS Code (bottom-left corner) now shows **`v1`**: you are on the v1 branch
3. Add a file, e.g., `v1_branch_edition.md` → **Commit to v1**
4. You see **"Publish branch"** instead of "Push". **Why?**
   → The branch exists **only locally**. It must be **published** to the remote first, then you can push to it.
5. **Switch back to `master`** → the new file is **not there!** ✅ That's the point of branches.

### 8.3 Pull Request (PR) & Merge

**Pull Request** = you **request the owner of the master branch to *pull* your code from your branch into master.**

> 🤔 Confusing name? You're not "pulling" anything. You're **asking the owner to pull** your changes in. That's why it's called a *pull request*.

**Steps:**
1. Push your branch → GitHub shows the green **"Compare & pull request"** button
2. Write a title/description (tutor's joke: *"Hey boss, I need at least a 25% hike"* 😄)
3. Check the arrow direction: **`v1 → master`**
4. **Create pull request**
5. The **owner/approver** reviews → **Merge** (or rejects with feedback)
6. After merging → **delete the branch** (it's no longer needed)

**Who approves PRs?**
- **Your own repo:** you (the owner)
- **In a company:** the **repo owner / admins / senior developers / the client**
  - *Tutor's example:* working for a client, the **client owns the repo**. They approve → code goes to production. Otherwise, you get feedback.

> 💡 PRs can be created in GitHub Desktop too, but it's **safer to do it in the browser**. You'll always have browser access to GitHub.

### 8.4 Feature Branch

**Every feature gets its own branch**, so:
- You can develop **in peace** (you're the only one changing it)
- Others working on main are **not disturbed**
- At the end → **PR → merge**

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 8 — Branches**

# 📌 TOPIC 9 — Contributing to Open-Source Projects

### 9.1 Why Contribute?

- Example: **PyTorch** on GitHub has **5,000+ open issues** and only about **5,000 contributors** (tiny compared to millions of developers).
- Solve a good issue → become a **contributor** → *"Contributor at PyTorch"* looks great on your resume.

**How to find a starting point:** filter issues by the label **`good first issue`**. These are easier issues for beginners.

> ⚠️ **Sincere request from the tutor:** Don't make **useless PRs** that only fix a spelling or grammar mistake in a README just to become a "contributor". It looks bad. **Make a meaningful contribution.**

### 9.2 Can AI Contribute to Open Source Entirely?

**Partially, but not fully. Why?**
- **AI is not free; it is very expensive.**
- Open-source repos are **giant codebases** → solving a hard issue needs **a lot of compute**.
- Nobody is paying to run AI on every issue.
- Running AI locally is also hard: the tutor ran a **~27B-parameter open-source model** on an **RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM)** and it was **not fast enough** for real work. Even the 4-bit version needs ~17 GB VRAM.
- You *can* try fixing basic issues with an AI coding agent if you have the budget.

**Who approves PRs in open source?** A list of **approvers (senior maintainers)**. Before they review, **automated tests** run on every push.

### 9.3 Step-by-Step: Fork → Clone → Change → Push → Pull Request

![Open-source contribution flow](images/git_open_source_flow.png)

| Step | Action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **① Fork** | Click **Fork** on the original repo | Creates a **copy of the entire repo on YOUR account**. You **can't push** to someone else's repo because you don't own it. |
| **② Clone** | Clone **your fork** to your computer | To work locally |
| **③ Change** | Fix the bug / add the feature in VS Code | The actual contribution |
| **④ Commit & Push** | Commit and push to **your fork** | Only **your fork** is updated, **not** the original |
| **⑤ Pull Request** | Open a PR from your fork → original repo | Ask the owner to **pull your changes** into their repo |

The owner can **merge** it (→ you become a contributor) or reject it. **It's their choice.**

**Practice repo:** `octocat/Spoon-Knife`, made by GitHub (**Octocat** is GitHub's mascot) **just for practising** forks and PRs.

**Sync fork:** If your fork falls **behind** the original repo, click **"Sync fork"** on GitHub to update it.

**Update a local clone:** use **Fetch origin** (GitHub Desktop) or `git fetch` / `git pull`.

### 9.4 Learner Question: How Do I Actually Fix an Issue?

> *"Once we choose an issue, how do we go ahead? Have it locally, understand the code, fix it, test locally, and push the code for a PR?"*

**Yes, exactly.** The full workflow:
1. Pick an issue (start with `good first issue`); read the repo's **CONTRIBUTING.md**
2. **Fork** → **clone** your fork
3. Create a **new branch** for the fix
4. **Understand the code** and reproduce the bug locally
5. **Fix it** and **run the tests locally**
6. **Commit → push** to your fork
7. Open a **Pull Request** and mention the issue number (e.g., *"Fixes #1234"*)
8. **Automated tests** run → **maintainers review** → merge (or feedback)

### 9.5 🏠 Homework

1. **Fork** the tutor's class repository
2. In the **`students/`** folder, create a folder with **your name** (e.g., `students/Shivam_Prasad/`) and **add a file** inside it (remember: empty folders aren't tracked)
3. **Commit & push** to your fork
4. Create a **Pull Request** to the tutor's repo → once it's approved, **you become a contributor!**

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 9 — Contributing to Open-Source Projects**

# 📌 TOPIC 10 — Merge Conflicts & How to Resolve Them

### 10.1 What Is a Conflict? The Chocolate Cake Example 🍫

![Merge conflict](images/git_merge_conflict.png)

- The **chef** has a chocolate cake recipe (= **main branch**). One step says **white sugar**.
- **You** take a copy of the recipe and experiment: replace white sugar with **stevia**.
- Your **sibling** also takes a copy and replaces white sugar with **honey**.
- Both of you try to put your version back into the chef's recipe.
- **Same line, two different changes** → Git **can't decide** which one is right → **CONFLICT**.

> **A conflict happens when two branches change the SAME line of the SAME file differently.**
> If they change *different* lines or files, Git merges automatically with no conflict.

### 10.2 What a Conflict Looks Like

Git marks the conflicting part of the file like this:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD          (your version)
sugar = stevia
=======
sugar = honey
>>>>>>> sibling-branch  (the incoming version)
```

### 10.3 How to Resolve It

1. **Open the file**. VS Code highlights the conflict with buttons: **Accept Current / Accept Incoming / Accept Both**
2. **Decide** what the final line should be (keep yours, keep theirs, or combine them)
3. **Delete the markers** (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`)
4. **Save**, then **`git add`** the file → **`git commit`**
5. Push. The merge is complete ✅

> 💡 **Avoid conflicts:** pull often, keep branches short-lived, and talk to teammates working on the same files.

*(Note: the transcript was cut off in the middle of this example. Sections 10.2–10.3 use the standard Git way to resolve conflicts.)*

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 10 — Merge Conflicts & How to Resolve Them**

# 📌 TOPIC 11 — Bonus: Terminal Cheat Sheet (GitHub Desktop → Terminal)

Future classes use **only the terminal**, so here is what each GitHub Desktop button does as a command:

| GitHub Desktop button | Terminal command |
|---|---|
| Add → Clone repository | `git clone <repo-url>` |
| (changed files list) | `git status` |
| Tick files to include | `git add <file>`  or  `git add .` |
| Commit to `<branch>` | `git commit -m "message"` |
| Push origin | `git push` |
| Fetch origin | `git fetch` |
| Pull origin | `git pull` |
| New branch | `git switch -c v1` |
| Switch branch | `git switch master` |
| Publish branch | `git push -u origin v1` |
| History tab | `git log --oneline` |
| Merge into current branch | `git merge v1` |
| Delete branch | `git branch -d v1` |

**A typical day:**

```bash
git pull                          # get latest code
git switch -c feature-login       # new feature branch
# ... edit files ...
git add .
git commit -m "Add login page"
git push -u origin feature-login  # then open a Pull Request on GitHub
```

# 📌 TOPIC 12 — Recap & Extra Facts (covered at the start of Class 3)

### 12.1 `main` vs `master`

- Some repos call the default branch **`master`**, others **`main`**.
- **There is no technical difference.** They are just two names for the same thing (the stable branch).
- *Extra fact:* GitHub changed the default name for new repos from `master` to `main` in 2020. Older repos still use `master`.

### 12.2 Code Stays Remote: GitHub Codespaces

- In the past, every project had a **local** repo + a **remote** repo.
- Today, **many companies keep code remote-only for security**. Nothing is cloned to your laptop.
- **GitHub Codespaces** = a full coding environment (VS Code) that runs **in the cloud, in your browser**. *(Tutor will cover it later.)*

### 12.3 Conflict Recap

- You clone/branch the repo and start working.
- Meanwhile **master changes** (other people merge their work).
- Now your copy and master **disagree** → you must **merge master's changes into yours** and fix the clashing lines. That is **resolving the conflict** (Topic 10).

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 12 — Recap & Extra Facts (covered at the start of Class 3)**

# 📌 TOPIC 13 — Git from the Terminal (No UI)

> 💡 Git is a **very deep hole**. About **4–5 commands cover 90% of real work**. The tutor remembers about **10 commands**, no more. Don't over-study it.

### 13.1 Install Git

```bash
sudo apt install git     # Linux (Ubuntu)
brew install git         # Mac
```

### 13.2 Tell Git Who You Are (one time)

```bash
git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

### 13.3 Authenticate with GitHub: SSH Keys

- **Old way (~5 years ago):** type your **username + password on every push**.
- **New way:** an **SSH key pair**. Much **more secure**, and no typing passwords every time.

```
Your computer                          GitHub
┌──────────────────┐                   ┌──────────────────────────┐
│ PRIVATE key 🔒    │ ◄── they match ──► │ PUBLIC key (you upload)  │
│ (never share it) │                   │ Settings → SSH & GPG keys│
└──────────────────┘                   └──────────────────────────┘
```

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"   # 1. create the key pair
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                     # 2. copy the PUBLIC key
# 3. GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → paste
ssh -T git@github.com                         # 4. test the connection
```

> ⚠️ The **private key** (`id_ed25519`, no `.pub`) must **never** be shared or shown on screen.

### 13.4 Full Demo: New Repo → First Push (terminal only)

```bash
# 1. On GitHub: New → name it (e.g. "September-21-MLOps") → Public → Create → copy the URL
git clone <repo-url>          # 2. local copy
cd September-21-MLOps
ls                            # empty folder
touch something.txt           # 3. create a file
git add .                     # 4. stage ALL changed files
git commit -m "First commit"  # 5. snapshot (local)
git push                      # 6. upload to GitHub
```

> 💡 For a **brand-new branch** that doesn't exist on GitHub yet, the first push needs an **upstream**:
> `git push -u origin <branch-name>` (the terminal version of **"Publish branch"**).

### 13.5 The Big Three (used over and over)

```
git add .   →   git commit -m "message"   →   git push
```

For **every** new change: **add → commit → push**.

| Want to stage… | Command |
|---|---|
| Everything | `git add .` |
| One file | `git add something.txt` |
| One folder | `git add lec-1/` |

> ⚠️ **Golden rule: `git pull` before `git push`.** Someone else may have pushed changes. Get them first, or your push can be rejected/conflict.

### 13.6 Tutor's Lazy Shortcut: One Command for All Three

The tutor wrote a small **shell function** in their terminal config that runs add + commit + push in one go. The text you type becomes the commit message. *"Just different ways of being lazy."* 😄

```bash
# add to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc
gacp() { git add . && git commit -m "$1" && git push; }

gacp "Add login page"     # = add + commit + push
```

*(The function name has no special meaning. It's whatever name you give it. The tutor also has one for `git log`.)*

### 13.7 See What's Going On: `status`, `log`, `diff`

| Command | Shows |
|---|---|
| `git status` | Which files are changed / staged / not tracked |
| `git log` | All past commits: **author, email, date/time, message** |
| `git log --oneline` | Short version: one line per commit |
| `git diff` | **Exact line changes** you made that are **not staged/committed yet** |
| `git diff <file>` | Changes in **one particular file** |

### 13.8 💡 Weak at Linux Terminal Commands?

The tutor recommends a **~5-hour Linux command-line course on YouTube**. **Don't** watch it in one go. Do **30–60 minutes a day** or an hour on weekends.

> *"You will never be as free and less stressed than you are right now."* Practise now.

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 13 — Git from the Terminal (No UI)**

# 📌 TOPIC 14 — Git Rebase

![Git rebase: before and after](images/git_rebase.png)

### 14.1 The Situation

- You create a feature branch **`v1`** from `main` and work on it.
- **Meanwhile, others keep committing to `main`.**
- So `main` now has commits that **`v1` doesn't have**.

### 14.2 What Rebase Does

**Re-base** = change the **base** of your branch.
It **lifts all your `v1` commits** and **replays them on the tip (latest commit) of `main`**, as if you had started `v1` today.

```bash
git switch v1          # be on your feature branch
git rebase main        # move v1 on top of the latest main
# conflict? → fix the file → git add <file> → git rebase --continue
# want to cancel?       → git rebase --abort
```

### 14.3 Merge vs Rebase

| | `git merge` | `git rebase` |
|---|---|---|
| History shape | Branches stay visible (a "fork" in the tree) | **One straight line** (linear) |
| Commit history | **Kept as it really happened** | **Rewritten**: your commits become new commits |
| Final code | Same | Same |
| Safe for shared branches? | ✅ Yes | ⚠️ Risky |

### 14.4 Why People Like It, and Why the Tutor Doesn't Recommend It

- ✅ **Pro:** people like **linear trees**. They're cleaner and easier to read.
- ❌ **Con:** rebase **re-commits every commit**, so it **rewrites commit history**. You **lose information**, like **when the feature was originally developed**. That's not good.
- *Extra golden rule:* **never rebase a branch other people are also using.** Their history won't match yours anymore.

> **Learner question:** *What if there's a conflict during rebase?*
> **Answer:** Solve it exactly the same way as in Topic 10: fix the lines, `git add`, continue.

> ✅ **END OF TOPIC 14 — Git Rebase**

## Quick Revision

| Term | Easy Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Git** | Open-source version control system (the technology) |
| **GitHub** | Microsoft's product that hosts Git repos online (like Gmail for email) |
| **Git services** | GitHub (Microsoft), GitLab (GitLab Inc.), Bitbucket (Atlassian), CodeCommit (AWS) |
| **Commit** | Save a snapshot of the codebase in the **local** repo |
| **Centralized VCS** | One server, one copy, one person at a time; very secure but a single point of failure, not scalable, no offline work |
| **Distributed VCS** | Everyone has a full copy; scalable and works offline; risk = code leaks (GTA 5 leak) |
| **Repository** | Fancy word for a folder of code/documents |
| **Local repo** | The copy on your computer |
| **Remote repo** | The online copy (GitHub) |
| **add** | Put file(s) in the staging area |
| **Staging area** | The "waiting room" of files picked for the next commit |
| **push** | Upload local commits to the remote repo |
| **fetch** | Download remote changes (doesn't change your files) |
| **pull** | Update local with remote (fetch + merge) |
| **clone** | Make a local copy of a remote repo |
| **Flow** | ADD → COMMIT → PUSH |
| **GitHub profile** | Your real portfolio; pin projects, add UI screenshots, avoid walls of text |
| **README** | Window into a project: problem, approach, quick start |
| **.gitkeep** | Placeholder file so Git tracks an empty folder |
| **Branch** | A copy of the codebase to work on safely without touching main |
| **Publish branch** | A new branch exists only locally until it's published to the remote |
| **Pull Request** | Asking the owner to pull your branch's code into main |
| **Merge** | Combine a branch into main (after PR approval) |
| **Feature branch** | One branch per feature, so you develop in peace |
| **Fork** | Copy of someone else's repo onto **your** account |
| **Open-source flow** | Fork → Clone → Change → Commit & Push (to fork) → Pull Request |
| **Sync fork** | Update your fork when it falls behind the original |
| **good first issue** | Beginner-friendly issues in open-source repos |
| **Conflict** | Two branches changed the same line differently → a human must choose |
| **Resolve conflict** | Pick/combine → remove `<<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>>` → add → commit |
| **Why terminal?** | Remote servers have no UI, only a terminal |
| **main vs master** | Same thing, two names for the default/stable branch |
| **Codespaces** | GitHub's cloud coding environment; code never sits on your laptop |
| **git config** | Set your name + email once |
| **SSH key** | Private key on your PC + public key on GitHub → secure login, no password per push |
| **Big three** | `git add .` → `git commit -m "msg"` → `git push` |
| **Pull before push** | Always get others' changes first |
| **Upstream (`-u`)** | First push of a new branch: `git push -u origin <branch>` |
| **git status** | What's changed / staged |
| **git log** | Commit history (author, email, time, message) |
| **git diff** | Line-by-line changes not yet committed |
| **Rebase** | Replay your branch's commits on the tip of main → linear history |
| **Why avoid rebase** | Rewrites commit history → lose when work really happened |
